faq.q: Why does starting ART sometimes improve platelet count?

exam: A 32‑year‑old woman with HIV (CD4 150) presents with petechiae and platelet count 45 ×10⁹/L. What is your next step? — Review ART adherence, order malaria smear, start prednisone if no infection found.
How does HIV‑associated thrombocytopenia differ from drug‑induced thrombocytopenia? — Timing with drug exposure, reversibility on withdrawal, and presence of immune markers.
A patient on zidovudine has platelets 90 ×10⁹/L. Should you stop the drug? — Consider other causes first; if platelets fall <50 ×10⁹/L or bleeding occurs, switch to an alternative ART.
What laboratory test helps distinguish immune thrombocytopenia from DIC? — Coagulation profile (PT/aPTT, fibrinogen, D‑dimer); normal results favor immune cause.

In a resource‑limited setting without IVIG, how would you manage severe bleeding with platelets 15 ×10⁹/L? — Give high‑dose steroids, transfuse platelets, treat any identifiable infection, and consider tranexamic acid.
Why is platelet transfusion alone insufficient in HIV‑associated thrombocytopenia? — Auto‑antibodies rapidly destroy transfused platelets; underlying immune process must be suppressed.
What are the key red‑flag signs that require urgent referral? — Active intracranial bleed, platelet <20 ×10⁹/L with mucosal hemorrhage, sudden platelet drop >50 %.
How does malaria co‑infection modify the management of HIV‑related thrombocytopenia? — Treat malaria promptly; platelet count often improves after parasite clearance.
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Immune‑mediated low platelet count in people living with HIV, often mild to moderate, may cause bleeding or be a marker of disease progression. Diagnosis requires exclusion of other causes common in low‑resource settings.

b: Platelet count <150 ×10⁹/L defines thrombocytopenia
Mild (100‑150), moderate (50‑100), severe (<50) ×10⁹/L
sections.p: Thrombocytopenia in HIV is usually immune‑mediated, caused by auto‑antibodies against platelets or megakaryocytes. It can appear at any CD4 count, but is more frequent when CD4 <200 cells/µL.

t.b: Is the platelet count low and are other lineages affected? → Isolated thrombocytopenia suggests HIV‑related or drug‑induced cause.
Are platelets clumped or abnormal? → Excludes pseudothrombocytopenia and shows platelet morphology.
What is the immune status? → High viral load or low CD4 supports HIV‑related mechanism.

t.a: Serology for hepatitis B/C, malaria smear, TB sputum
t.b: Are co‑infections present? → Co‑infection can cause secondary thrombocytopenia.
Is marrow production suppressed? → Helps rule out marrow infiltration or aplasia.

b: Auto‑antibodies (IgG) bind platelet glycoproteins → splenic sequestration
HIV infects megakaryocyte precursors → reduced output
Cytokine storm (TNF‑α, IL‑6) shortens platelet lifespan
sections.p: The problem lies in peripheral platelet destruction and impaired production. Immune complexes, direct HIV infection of megakaryocytes, and cytokine dysregulation all contribute.

b: Petechiae, purpura, mucosal bleeding
Exacerbated bleeding after minor trauma or surgery
May herald HIV disease progression
sections.p: Most patients are asymptomatic; bleeding appears when platelets fall <20 ×10⁹/L. In low‑resource settings, severe thrombocytopenia can be fatal if untreated, especially with co‑existing malaria or TB.

b: Ask about antiretroviral regimen – zidovudine, protease inhibitors can lower platelets
Look for fever, splenomegaly – suggest malaria or TB
Check coagulation profile – normal PT/aPTT points to isolated thrombocytopenia
sections.p: Examiners often test your ability to differentiate HIV‑associated thrombocytopenia from drug‑induced, malaria‑related, or disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).

b: Missing malaria smear when patient has fever and thrombocytopenia
Prescribing NSAIDs that worsen bleeding risk
Ignoring a rising viral load as a trigger for immune thrombocytopenia
sections.p: Avoid assuming all low platelets in HIV are drug‑related; always rule out co‑infections and nutritional deficiencies common locally.

b: Optimize ART – improve immune control, often raises platelets
IVIG 1 g/kg ×2 days if rapid rise needed or steroids contraindicated
Platelet transfusion only if <20 ×10⁹/L with active bleeding
Avoid aspirin, NSAIDs, and warfarin unless absolutely necessary
sections.p: Treat the underlying HIV, control co‑infections, and provide supportive care. First‑line specific therapy is corticosteroids; IVIG is reserved for severe bleeding or steroid failure.

b: Malaria‑induced thrombocytopenia – usually accompanied by fever, parasites on smear
Drug‑induced thrombocytopenia – temporal relation to new meds, resolves after withdrawal
DIC – prolonged PT/aPTT, elevated D‑dimer, fibrinogen low
sections.p: Conditions that also cause isolated low platelets in similar settings.

b: Normal PT/aPTT does not rule out early DIC
Low hemoglobin may mask bleeding source
sections.p: Platelet clumping on EDTA tubes can falsely lower counts; repeat with citrate if smear shows aggregates.

whenToSeekHelp: Platelet count <20 ×10⁹/L with active mucosal or intracranial bleeding
Sudden drop >50 % in platelets within 24 h
Unexplained severe headache or neurological deficit
